rv.q: She is sensational, balancing gawky comedy with a yearning for a life unlived through duty and misfortune.

Given that the book is more a collection of sketches, the production nimbly sews the fabric together, making discreet cuts here and there (Captain Brown and his fatal railway accident are dropped altogether).
At Richmond’s Orange Tree Theatre, Elizabeth Gaskell’s Cranford is brought to life in a gloriously funny production that is a joy from start to finish.

What emerges is a wonderfully concise and coherent work of theatre, the roots of which are clear, but the substance very much of their own making, of an intimate space managed perfectly, of women now and not just then.
A phenomenal cast and crisp direction combine to provide an equally hilarious and thoughtful theatrical experience.
But with only lip service paid to the broader social context in which these women lived, much of what could be interesting here dances tantalisingly beneath the surface.
It is a long time since I’ve seen a show that is simultaneously so trenchant and so funny, and which sends the audience out of the theatre with such a warm, seasonal glow.
This cosy and humorous production is a delightful few hours in the theatre.
For a few short hours, the wonderful Orange Tree Theatre takes us there.
The exceptional writing, direction and performances allow the comedy and tragedy to ebb and flow in a beautiful example of what theatre can achieve.
This warm-hearted adaptation from director Josh Roche offers tender reflections on grief and independence while maximising the laughs.
Lin Coghlan and Shaun McKenna’s adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell's 'Cranford' balances sharp comedy with tender heartbreak, led by an unforgettable Tamsin Greig.
It’s otherwise flawless, what one comes to expect of the Orange Tree (at Christmas or any other time), in this Tom Littler’s final year as Artistic Director.
This is a seasonal offering, and the play’s resolve is utterly heartwarming and elevating.
Still, there are enough pleasing elements in Josh Roche’s lively, speedy production to make for an enjoyable evening.

cn.t: Cranford earns near-universal acclaim at the Orange Tree, with Tamsin Greig's performance drawing particular praise. A handful of critics find the festive sentimentality overwhelming, but most celebrate its sharp comedy and emotional depth.
